## An integral is a probability-weighted average

Before working with a continuous posterior, imagine only three possible parameter values:
$0.1$, $0.3$ and $0.6$, with posterior probabilities $0.2$, $0.5$ and $0.3$.
The posterior mean is

$$0.2(0.1)+0.5(0.3)+0.3(0.6)=0.35.$$

The probability that the parameter exceeds $0.4$ is $0.3$: only the last possibility
satisfies the event. We obtained two answers from the same posterior by changing what we
average. For a mean, average the parameter itself. For an event probability, average a
variable that equals one when the event holds and zero otherwise.

With a continuous parameter, a small interval of width $\Delta$ near $\theta_j$ has
probability approximately $p(\theta_j\mid y)\Delta$. The corresponding weighted sum is
$\sum_j g(\theta_j)p(\theta_j\mid y)\Delta$. Making the intervals finer gives the
integral below. The function $g$ simply records the question we are asking.

Monte Carlo uses a different way to represent the probabilities. In a large sample from
our three-point posterior, roughly 20% of draws equal $0.1$, 50% equal $0.3$ and 30%
equal $0.6$. Their **unweighted** average already incorporates the posterior probabilities
through those frequencies. Weighting those draws by the posterior again would count it
twice. Importance weights become necessary only when draws instead come from a different
distribution. Keep this distinction in mind when we introduce the two estimators.

## Why posterior expectations are integrals

Lecture 1 ended on a specific complaint: the grid trick that solved the coin-tossing
problem without algebra needs $G^d$ evaluations for $d$ parameters on a $G$-point grid,
so a five-parameter model already needs billions of evaluations and a ten-parameter one
is simply out of reach. This lecture picks up exactly there, because the underlying
problem never went away. Every quantity we report from a posterior is an integral. The
posterior mean is $\mathbb{E}[\theta \mid y] = \int \theta\, p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta$,
a predictive mean is $\int g(\theta)\, p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta$ for some function $g$,
and a tail probability such as $\Pr(\theta > c \mid y)$ is the expectation of an
indicator function, $\int \mathbf{1}\{\theta > c\}\, p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta$. Every
one of these has the same shape,

$$
\mathbb{E}_{p}[g(\theta)] \;=\; \int g(\theta)\, p(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta ,
$$

for some choice of $g$: the identity function for a mean, an indicator for a
probability, a squared deviation for a variance. In the conjugate models of Lecture 1
these integrals had closed forms because we could recognise the kernel. That was a
consequence of the chosen distribution families. A higher-dimensional conjugate model
can still have analytic answers, as the regression model showed. With other prior and
likelihood combinations, the required integral may lack a convenient closed form.
Regular-grid quadrature remains useful in low dimensions, but its number of evaluation
points grows exponentially with dimension. Monte Carlo offers a different approximation
whose error is governed by variation in the quantity we are estimating.

The resolution is to stop trying to cover the whole parameter space with points and
instead put points where the posterior actually has mass, by drawing random samples
from it. This lecture builds that idea from the ground up: plain Monte Carlo
integration and its error, the importance-sampling trick for when we cannot sample the
posterior directly, rejection sampling as an alternative that produces exact draws, and
sampling-importance-resampling as the bridge to the Markov chain methods of the next
two lectures. We close with two applied examples, a gamma model for a positive-valued
series with a genuinely non-conjugate posterior, and an option-pricing simulator in
which the volatility itself carries posterior uncertainty.

We import the usual libraries, add the one new function this lecture needs for
numerical integration, and fix the seed.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from scipy.integrate import quad
from scipy.special import gammaln
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})
```

## Monte Carlo integration and the law of large numbers

Suppose we can draw independent samples $\theta^{(1)}, \dots, \theta^{(S)}$ from the
posterior $p(\theta \mid y)$. The **Monte Carlo estimator** of
$\mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)]$ replaces the integral by the sample average of $g$ evaluated
at the draws,

$$
\hat{g}_S \;=\; \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S} g\big(\theta^{(s)}\big).
$$

Two facts justify treating this average as an estimate of the integral, and both are
worth deriving rather than asserting, because the whole lecture rests on them.
**Unbiasedness** follows from linearity of expectation together with the fact that
each $\theta^{(s)}$ is itself a draw from $p$:

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{g}_S\big]
= \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S g(\theta^{(s)})\right]
= \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \mathbb{E}\big[g(\theta^{(s)})\big]
= \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)]
= \mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)] .
$$

The estimator is centred on the right answer for every $S$, not just in the limit.
**Consistency** is the law of large numbers: as $S \to \infty$, $\hat{g}_S \to
\mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)]$ with probability one, for essentially any $g$ with finite
variance under $p$. Crucially, nothing in either derivation refers to the dimension of
$\theta$. Unbiasedness holds term by term regardless of how many components $\theta$
has, and the law of large numbers is a statement about a one-dimensional sequence of
numbers $g(\theta^{(1)}), g(\theta^{(2)}), \dots$, whatever the dimension of the object
that produced them. This is the entire reason simulation escapes the curse of
dimensionality that sank the grid.

To see the machinery reproduce a known answer, we return to the coin from Lecture 1:
nine heads in twelve tosses with a $\text{Beta}(5,5)$ prior, giving the exact posterior
$\theta \mid y \sim \text{Beta}(14, 8)$ with mean $14/22 \approx 0.6364$ and
$\Pr(\theta > 0.5 \mid y) \approx 0.905$. Because this posterior is available in closed
form we can sample it directly with `scipy.stats`, which lets us check the Monte Carlo
answer against the value we already trust before using simulation anywhere it matters.

```{python}
a, b, y, n = 5, 5, 9, 12
posterior = stats.beta(a + y, b + n - y)          # Beta(14, 8), exact

c = 0.5
true_mean = posterior.mean()
true_tail = 1 - posterior.cdf(c)

S = 5000
draws = posterior.rvs(size=S, random_state=rng)

mc_mean = draws.mean()
mc_tail = np.mean(draws > c)

print(f"posterior mean    exact {true_mean:.4f}   MC {mc_mean:.4f}")
print(f"P(theta > {c})     exact {true_tail:.4f}   MC {mc_tail:.4f}")
```

Both Monte Carlo estimates land within a few thousandths of the values Lecture 1
derived by hand. The tail probability is nothing but the average of an indicator
variable, so the identical averaging machine handles a mean, a probability, a
variance, or any other posterior summary without a single new idea; only the function
$g$ inside the sum changes.

## Where the error comes from: the Monte Carlo standard error

A Monte Carlo estimate is a random number computed from a finite sample, so it needs an
error bar exactly as an estimator computed from data does. Write $\sigma_g^2 =
\operatorname{Var}_p[g(\theta)]$ for the posterior variance of $g(\theta)$, assumed
finite. Because the terms $g(\theta^{(1)}), \dots, g(\theta^{(S)})$ are independent and
identically distributed, the variance of their average follows from the rule for the
variance of a sum of independent terms,

$$
\operatorname{Var}\big[\hat{g}_S\big]
= \operatorname{Var}\left[\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S g(\theta^{(s)})\right]
= \frac{1}{S^2}\sum_{s=1}^S \operatorname{Var}\big[g(\theta^{(s)})\big]
= \frac{1}{S^2} \cdot S\sigma_g^2
= \frac{\sigma_g^2}{S} .
$$

Because $\hat{g}_S$ is itself an average of $S$ independent, identically distributed
terms with finite variance, the central limit theorem applies to it directly, giving

$$
\hat{g}_S \; \overset{\text{approx}}{\sim} \; \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)],
\; \frac{\sigma_g^2}{S}\right)
\qquad \text{for large } S,
$$

so the standard deviation of the estimator, the **Monte Carlo standard error**, is

$$
\text{MCSE} = \frac{\sigma_g}{\sqrt{S}} \;\approx\; \frac{\hat\sigma_g}{\sqrt{S}},
$$

with $\hat\sigma_g$ the sample standard deviation of the $g(\theta^{(s)})$ substituted
for the unknown $\sigma_g$. The $\sqrt{S}$ in the denominator is the single most
important fact about Monte Carlo methods in practice: the error shrinks with the square
root of the number of draws, not with the number of draws itself. Halving the MCSE
needs four times as many draws, and adding one decimal digit of accuracy needs a
hundred times as many. The estimator is unbiased and it does converge, but the rate is
unforgiving, and this is the fact every later chapter's "how many draws do we need"
question comes back to.

```{python}
mcse_mean = draws.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(S)
print(f"MC mean {mc_mean:.4f}  +/- {1.96*mcse_mean:.4f}  (95% MC interval)")

ind = (draws > c).astype(float)                  # g(theta) = 1{theta > c}
mcse_tail = ind.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(S)
print(f"MC tail {mc_tail:.4f}  +/- {1.96*mcse_tail:.4f}  (95% MC interval)")
```

The two intervals reported here describe uncertainty in the *Monte Carlo estimate*
coming from having drawn only $S$ values, not uncertainty about $\theta$ itself, which
is already fully captured by the posterior. Drawing more samples narrows these
intervals arbitrarily; it changes nothing about the posterior, which is fixed once the
data and the prior are fixed. Note also that the tail-probability MCSE is noticeably
larger relative to its estimate than the mean's MCSE is: an indicator has a Bernoulli
variance $p(1-p)$, so the relative error of a rare-event probability is much worse than
that of a well-centred mean at the same $S$, a point the exercises return to.

### Watching the $1/\sqrt{S}$ rate

The clearest way to internalise the square-root rate is to watch the running average as
draws accumulate, with a band of width $\pm 1.96 \times \text{MCSE}$ around the known
posterior mean. The running estimate should wander inside a band that narrows steadily,
never settling but converging.

```{python}
running_mean = np.cumsum(draws) / np.arange(1, S + 1)
s_grid = np.arange(1, S + 1)
band = 1.96 * posterior.std() / np.sqrt(s_grid)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(s_grid, running_mean, lw=1, label="running MC estimate")
ax.axhline(true_mean, color="black", lw=1, ls=":", label="true posterior mean")
ax.fill_between(s_grid, true_mean - band, true_mean + band,
                alpha=0.2, label=r"true mean $\pm\,1.96\,$MCSE")
ax.set_xlabel("number of draws  S"); ax.set_ylabel("estimate of posterior mean")
ax.set_ylim(true_mean - 0.15, true_mean + 0.15)
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Monte Carlo estimate converges at rate 1/sqrt(S)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The band visibly narrows as $S$ grows and the running average stays inside it, which is
the derivation above made concrete. To confirm the rate rather than merely gesture at
it, we can measure the actual root-mean-squared error of the estimator over many
independent repetitions at a range of sample sizes and check that it falls in
proportion to $1/\sqrt{S}$, which on a log-log plot is a straight line of slope
$-1/2$.

```{python}
sizes = np.array([50, 200, 800, 3200, 12800])
reps = 200
rmse = np.empty(len(sizes))
for i, m in enumerate(sizes):
    ests = np.array([posterior.rvs(size=m, random_state=rng).mean()
                      for _ in range(reps)])
    rmse[i] = np.sqrt(np.mean((ests - true_mean) ** 2))

ref = rmse[0] * np.sqrt(sizes[0] / sizes)         # 1/sqrt(S) reference line

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.loglog(sizes, rmse, "o-", label="empirical RMSE")
ax.loglog(sizes, ref, "--", color="grey", label=r"$\propto 1/\sqrt{S}$ reference")
ax.set_xlabel("number of draws  S"); ax.set_ylabel("RMSE of MC estimate")
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Error falls like 1/sqrt(S) on a log-log scale")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The empirical curve sits on top of the reference line across three orders of magnitude
in $S$, which is the $\sqrt{S}$ law made visible rather than merely quoted: each step in
the grid of sizes multiplies $S$ by exactly 4, and the RMSE drops by a factor close to
2 at every step, exactly as $1/\sqrt{4} = 1/2$ predicts.

## Coin tossing revisited: when we cannot sample directly

Everything so far assumed we could draw straight from the posterior, which only worked
because the beta prior is conjugate to the binomial likelihood. Suppose instead we keep
the same coin and the same data, nine heads in twelve tosses, but replace the beta
prior with a **truncated normal** prior on $\theta \in (0,1)$, $\theta \sim
\mathcal{N}(0.5, 1)$ restricted to the unit interval. This is a perfectly reasonable
prior belief, centred at a fair coin with the same spread as before, but it is not
conjugate to the binomial: multiplying the binomial likelihood by a normal density does
not produce a kernel we recognise, and the posterior is now

$$
p(\theta \mid y) \;\propto\; \theta^{9}(1-\theta)^{3} \times
\exp\!\left(-\frac{(\theta - 0.5)^2}{2}\right), \qquad 0 < \theta < 1 ,
$$

a shape with no name. We cannot sample it with `stats.beta.rvs` or any other canned
generator, and the normalising constant is a one-dimensional integral we happen to be
able to compute by quadrature here only because $\theta$ is scalar. We use that
quadrature once, as a ground truth to check the simulation methods against, exactly as
the closed-form beta posterior served as ground truth above.

```{python}
def unnorm_post(theta):
    return theta**9 * (1 - theta)**3 * stats.norm.pdf(theta, loc=0.5, scale=1.0)

Z, _ = quad(unnorm_post, 0, 1)                       # normalising constant
true_mean_tn, _ = quad(lambda t: t * unnorm_post(t) / Z, 0, 1)

grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(grid, unnorm_post(grid) / Z, label="posterior (truncated-normal prior)")
ax.axvline(true_mean_tn, color="grey", ls=":", label=f"mean = {true_mean_tn:.4f}")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta$"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("A non-conjugate posterior: no sampler exists for this shape")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The curve is a legitimate density, unimodal and shifted noticeably right of the prior's
0.5 by the nine observed heads, but it belongs to no textbook family. Quadrature
answered the one-dimensional question, and this is exactly where Lecture 1 warned we
would run out of road: with two or three parameters this same integral would need a
fine grid over each dimension, and the cost explodes long before an economically
interesting model is reached. What we need is a way to compute posterior expectations
under a density we can *evaluate* but not *sample*, without ever computing $Z$. That is
importance sampling.

## Importance sampling

The idea is to rewrite the target expectation as an expectation under a distribution we
*can* sample, called the **proposal** $q(\theta)$, by multiplying and dividing inside
the integral by $q$:

$$
\mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)]
= \int g(\theta)\, p(\theta)\, d\theta
= \int g(\theta)\, \frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)}\, q(\theta)\, d\theta
= \mathbb{E}_q\!\left[ g(\theta)\, w(\theta) \right],
\qquad w(\theta) = \frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)} ,
$$

valid whenever $q(\theta) > 0$ everywhere $g(\theta)p(\theta) \neq 0$. This is an exact
algebraic identity, not an approximation: it says the expectation of $g$ under $p$
equals the expectation of $g$ times a **importance weight** $w(\theta) = p(\theta) /
q(\theta)$ under $q$. Drawing $\theta^{(1)}, \dots, \theta^{(S)} \sim q$ and averaging
gives an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of this new expectation by exactly the same
argument as before, $\frac{1}{S}\sum_s g(\theta^{(s)}) w(\theta^{(s)})$.

In Bayesian work we almost never know $p(\theta) = p(\theta \mid y)$ exactly, only its
unnormalised kernel $\tilde p(\theta) = c \cdot p(\theta)$ for some unknown constant
$c$ (here, $c = Z$). Writing the weight in terms of the kernel introduces the same
unknown constant, $\tilde w(\theta) = \tilde p(\theta)/q(\theta) = c\, w(\theta)$, but
because it multiplies every weight identically, it cancels from a *ratio* of two
importance-sampling sums. This gives the **self-normalised** estimator,

$$
\hat{g}_S^{\,\text{IS}}
= \frac{\sum_{s=1}^{S} g(\theta^{(s)})\, \tilde{w}^{(s)}}
       {\sum_{s=1}^{S} \tilde{w}^{(s)}} ,
\qquad \tilde{w}^{(s)} = \frac{\tilde p(\theta^{(s)})}{q(\theta^{(s)})} ,
$$

which needs only the unnormalised target and works whether or not $Z$ is known. Unlike
the plain estimator, this one is a ratio of two Monte Carlo averages and is therefore
biased in finite samples, by an amount of order $1/S$: writing $\hat A_S =
\frac{1}{S}\sum_s g(\theta^{(s)})w(\theta^{(s)}) \to \mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)]$ and
$\hat B_S = \frac{1}{S}\sum_s w(\theta^{(s)}) \to 1$, the ratio $\hat A_S/\hat B_S$ is
not itself unbiased even though numerator and denominator separately are, because
$\mathbb{E}[\hat A_S/\hat B_S] \neq \mathbb{E}[\hat A_S]/\mathbb{E}[\hat B_S]$ in
general. What survives is consistency: both $\hat A_S$ and $\hat B_S$ converge almost
surely by the law of large numbers, so their ratio converges to $\mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)]
/ 1$ by the continuous mapping theorem. The self-normalised estimator trades a small,
vanishing bias for the ability to work with an unnormalised target, which in practice is
the only option we have.

We put this to work on the truncated-normal coin, proposing from a $\text{Uniform}(0,1)$
distribution, which covers the whole domain of $\theta$ generously.

```{python}
S_is = 20_000
prop = stats.uniform(0, 1)
samp = prop.rvs(size=S_is, random_state=rng)

w = unnorm_post(samp) / prop.pdf(samp)             # unnormalised weights
w_norm = w / w.sum()                               # self-normalised weights

is_mean = np.sum(samp * w_norm)
ess_good = 1.0 / np.sum(w_norm ** 2)
print(f"posterior mean    quadrature {true_mean_tn:.4f}   IS {is_mean:.4f}")
print(f"effective sample size: {ess_good:.0f} out of {S_is}")
```

The importance-sampling estimate lands within a few thousandths of the quadrature
answer, obtained entirely from uniform draws reweighted by the target's shape, with no
canned truncated-normal-times-binomial sampler anywhere in sight. The printed effective
sample size is explained next.

## The variance of the weights and effective sample size

Importance sampling is only as good as its weights are even. If a handful of draws
carry nearly all the weight, the weighted average behaves as though it were computed
from those few points alone, and its variance is far larger than a plain Monte Carlo
average over the same $S$ would give. This can be seen directly from the variance of a
single weighted term, $\operatorname{Var}_q[g(\theta)w(\theta)]$: substituting
$w = p/q$,

$$
\mathbb{E}_q\!\left[\big(g(\theta)w(\theta)\big)^2\right]
= \int g(\theta)^2 \frac{p(\theta)^2}{q(\theta)^2}\, q(\theta)\, d\theta
= \int g(\theta)^2\, w(\theta)\, p(\theta)\, d\theta
= \mathbb{E}_p\!\left[g(\theta)^2\, w(\theta)\right] ,
$$

so whenever $w(\theta)$ is large exactly where $g(\theta)^2 p(\theta)$ is not
negligible, the second moment — and hence the variance — of the importance-sampling
estimator inflates, even though the estimator's mean is unaffected. This happens
precisely when $q$ decays faster in the tails than $p$ does: then $w(\theta) =
p(\theta)/q(\theta) \to \infty$ as $\theta$ moves into the tail, and an occasional draw
that lands there is multiplied by an enormous weight. The standard diagnostic that
summarises how uneven the weights are is the **effective sample size**,

$$
\text{ESS} = \frac{\left(\sum_s \tilde{w}^{(s)}\right)^2}{\sum_s (\tilde{w}^{(s)})^2}
= \frac{1}{\sum_s (w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)})^2} ,
$$

which equals $S$ when all normalised weights are equal to $1/S$ and falls toward $1$
as one weight comes to dominate the rest; it is the number of *independent* posterior
draws the weighted sample is worth. The good uniform proposal above returned an ESS
of a bit over 40% of `S_is`: some efficiency is lost to reweighting, because a uniform
proposal still spends many draws away from where the posterior has its mass, but the
loss is moderate and the weights stay usable. We now deliberately choose a bad
proposal, one concentrated where the posterior has little mass, to see the failure
mode the derivation predicts.

```{python}
bad_prop = stats.beta(2, 10)                        # mass concentrated near small theta
samp_b = bad_prop.rvs(size=S_is, random_state=rng)
w_bad = unnorm_post(samp_b) / bad_prop.pdf(samp_b)
w_bad_norm = w_bad / w_bad.sum()

is_mean_bad = np.sum(samp_b * w_bad_norm)
ess_bad = 1.0 / np.sum(w_bad_norm ** 2)
print(f"bad-proposal mean estimate: {is_mean_bad:.4f}  (true {true_mean_tn:.4f})")
print(f"effective sample size: {ess_bad:.0f} out of {S_is}")
print(f"largest single normalised weight: {w_bad_norm.max():.3f}")
```

The posterior for this coin has almost all its mass between roughly $0.5$ and $0.9$,
while $\text{Beta}(2,10)$ concentrates near $0.15$: the proposal rarely visits the
region the target cares about, the rare draws that do land there receive very large
weights to compensate, and the effective sample size collapses to a small fraction of
`S_is`, with a single draw sometimes carrying a large share of the total weight. The
point estimate is visibly biased at this finite $S$ despite the theoretical guarantee
of consistency, because consistency is a statement about $S \to \infty$ and a
collapsed ESS means we are effectively very far from that limit. Plotting the two
weight distributions side by side shows the contrast directly.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8), sharey=True)
for ax, w_, ess_, ttl in [(axes[0], w_norm, ess_good, "good proposal (Uniform)"),
                          (axes[1], w_bad_norm, ess_bad, "bad proposal (Beta(2,10))")]:
    ax.hist(w_, bins=40, color="steelblue", alpha=0.85)
    ax.set_title(f"{ttl}\nESS = {ess_:.0f}")
    ax.set_xlabel("normalised weight")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
fig.suptitle("Importance weights: even vs degenerate")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The good proposal produces many small, comparable weights clustered together; the bad
one produces a spike of near-zero weights and a long thin tail of a few draws that
dominate the sum. The general lesson, and the reason importance sampling is taught
alongside a warning, is that a safe proposal needs **heavier tails than the target** and
must cover every region where the target has appreciable mass. A proposal that is too
narrow, or that decays faster than the target in some direction, produces a handful of
runaway weights and an estimator whose variance can be infinite even though its bias
vanishes asymptotically; the estimate looks perfectly reasonable until, on a bad draw of
the random seed, it suddenly is not. Finding such a proposal by hand becomes close to
impossible once $\theta$ has more than a few components, which is exactly the
difficulty that motivates the Markov chain samplers of the next two lectures.

## Rejection sampling

Importance sampling reweights every draw and never touches the target's normalising
constant, but its output is a set of *weighted* points, not a sample from $p$ itself.
**Rejection sampling** takes a different route to the same problem and returns actual,
unweighted draws from the target. Choose a proposal $q$ and a constant $M \geq 1$ such
that the **envelope condition**

$$
\tilde p(\theta) \;\leq\; M\, q(\theta) \qquad \text{for all } \theta
$$

holds, i.e. $M q$ lies everywhere above the unnormalised target. The algorithm then
repeats, for each draw wanted:

1. Generate a candidate $\tilde\theta \sim q(\theta)$.
2. Generate $u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$.
3. Accept $\theta = \tilde\theta$ if $u < \tilde p(\tilde\theta) / \big(M q(\tilde\theta)\big)$; otherwise discard $\tilde\theta$ and return to step 1.

The reason an accepted draw is an exact draw from $p$ is a short geometric argument
worth sketching in full. Consider the region under the envelope,
$\mathcal{A} = \{(\theta, u) : 0 \leq u \leq Mq(\theta)\}$. Steps 1 and 2 generate a
point uniformly distributed over $\mathcal{A}$: first $\theta$ from $q$, then, given
$\theta$, a height $u$ uniform on $[0, Mq(\theta)]$, which is precisely how a uniform
distribution on the region under a curve is built up. Step 3 keeps only the points that
additionally fall under the *target's* curve, $u < \tilde p(\theta)$, which by
construction lies entirely inside $\mathcal{A}$ because of the envelope condition. A
point drawn uniformly over a region and then restricted to a sub-region is uniformly
distributed over that sub-region, so the accepted $(\theta, u)$ pairs are uniform over
$\{(\theta,u) : 0 \le u \le \tilde p(\theta)\}$, and the marginal distribution of
$\theta$ under a uniform distribution on the area beneath a curve is exactly the density
proportional to that curve, namely $p(\theta)$. No reweighting is needed afterward
because the acceptance step already did the reweighting geometrically. The unconditional
acceptance probability at any single trial is $\Pr(\text{accept}) = \int \tilde
p(\theta)\,d\theta / M = Z/M$, so smaller $M$, meaning a tighter envelope, means fewer
wasted draws; this is also why the method reduces to plain Monte Carlo sampling when
$q = p$ exactly, since then $M = 1$ and every candidate is accepted.

We apply it to the truncated-normal coin with the same uniform proposal used for
importance sampling, generating candidates in batches so the loop terminates quickly.

```{python}
grid_M = np.linspace(1e-4, 1 - 1e-4, 2000)
M = (unnorm_post(grid_M) / prop.pdf(grid_M)).max()   # smallest valid envelope constant

N_target, accepted = 20_000, []
n_tried = 0
while len(accepted) < N_target:
    cand = prop.rvs(size=5000, random_state=rng)
    u = rng.uniform(size=cand.size)
    keep = u < unnorm_post(cand) / (M * prop.pdf(cand))
    accepted.extend(cand[keep])
    n_tried += cand.size

rej_draws = np.array(accepted[:N_target])
print(f"envelope constant M = {M:.3e}")
print(f"acceptance rate: {N_target/n_tried:.3f}  (theory: Z/M = {Z/M:.3f})")
print(f"rejection-sample mean: {rej_draws.mean():.4f}  (quadrature {true_mean_tn:.4f})")
```

The observed acceptance rate matches the theoretical $Z/M$ closely, and the mean of the
accepted draws reproduces the quadrature answer without any weight ever appearing in the
calculation: these are genuine, exchangeable draws from the posterior, usable in any
downstream calculation exactly like the direct beta draws from the first section. The
price is the acceptance rate itself. In one dimension an envelope constant a little
above one is usually attainable with a sensible proposal, but in $d$ dimensions the
volume between a safe envelope and the target typically grows so that $M$ grows
exponentially with $d$, and the acceptance rate $1/M$ collapses correspondingly:
rejection sampling suffers from the same curse of dimensionality as the grid, just with
a slower fuse.

## Sampling-importance-resampling

Importance sampling gives weighted points; rejection sampling gives unweighted points at
a cost that grows quickly with dimension. **Sampling-importance-resampling (SIR)**
is a cheap compromise that converts the weighted sample from importance sampling into an
approximately unweighted one, without needing an envelope constant at all. Having drawn
$\theta^{(1)}, \dots, \theta^{(S)} \sim q$ and computed self-normalised weights
$w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)}$, resample $N \leq S$ indices from $\{1, \dots, S\}$ with
replacement, using the weights as selection probabilities. A draw that received a large
weight is proportionally more likely to be copied into the resampled set, and one that
received a negligible weight is unlikely to appear at all, so the resulting sample
approximates a draw from $p$ itself the way rejection sampling delivers exactly. The
approximation improves as $S \to \infty$ with $N$ fixed, but unlike rejection sampling
it never rejects anything outright, so it costs no extra random draws beyond the
original importance sample.

```{python}
idx = rng.choice(S_is, size=S_is, replace=True, p=w_norm)
sir_draws = samp[idx]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(sir_draws, bins=40, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="SIR resample")
ax.plot(grid, unnorm_post(grid) / Z, lw=2, label="true posterior (quadrature)")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta$"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("SIR turns weighted draws into an (approximate) posterior sample")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"SIR resample mean: {sir_draws.mean():.4f}  (quadrature {true_mean_tn:.4f})")
```

The resampled histogram tracks the true density well because the original importance
sample here had a healthy effective sample size; with a degenerate weight distribution
like the bad proposal above, the same recipe would simply copy the same handful of
dominant points over and over, which is the resampling analogue of a collapsed ESS.
SIR is the conceptual bridge to Lectures 4 and 5: instead of reweighting a fixed
proposal once, Markov chain Monte Carlo methods let the sampler *adapt* its own
proposal as it explores the space, which is what makes them viable in high dimensions
where a single fixed $q$, however carefully chosen, cannot cover the target.

## A gamma model with no conjugate posterior

We close with two applications built entirely from the tools above. The first mirrors a
case used in Bayesian hydrology: a positive-valued series such as hourly glacier
meltwater discharge, modelled with a **gamma distribution**,
$Y \mid \nu, \lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(\nu, 1/\lambda)$ with shape $\nu$ and rate
$\lambda$, density $f(y \mid \nu, \lambda) = \frac{\lambda^\nu}{\Gamma(\nu)}
y^{\nu-1}e^{-\lambda y}$. There is no conjugate prior for the gamma family in both
parameters simultaneously, so we place a weakly informative prior directly, $\nu \sim
\text{Uniform}(0.1, 15)$ and $\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(2, 1)$ independent of $\nu$.
Given data $y_1,\dots,y_n$, the likelihood depends on the data only through the
sufficient statistics $n$, $\sum_i y_i$ and $\sum_i \log y_i$, so once those three
numbers are in hand, evaluating the likelihood at any candidate $(\nu, \lambda)$ costs
nothing further. We first simulate a discharge-like series so the true parameter values
are known and the exercise can be checked against them, then use **the prior itself as
the importance proposal**, a common shortcut for a first pass at a non-conjugate
posterior: because the unnormalised posterior is $\tilde p(\nu,\lambda) =
l(\nu,\lambda \mid y)\, p(\nu)p(\lambda)$ and the proposal is $q(\nu,\lambda) =
p(\nu)p(\lambda)$, the weight collapses to the likelihood itself,
$w(\nu,\lambda) = \tilde p/q = l(\nu,\lambda\mid y)$, so we need only draw from the
prior and weight by how well each draw explains the data.

```{python}
nu_true, lam_true, n_obs = 3.0, 2.0, 150
y_disch = rng.gamma(shape=nu_true, scale=1 / lam_true, size=n_obs)
sum_y, sum_logy = y_disch.sum(), np.log(y_disch).sum()

S_g = 400_000
nu_s = rng.uniform(0.1, 15, size=S_g)
lam_s = rng.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=1.0, size=S_g)

loglik = (n_obs * nu_s * np.log(lam_s) - n_obs * gammaln(nu_s)
          + (nu_s - 1) * sum_logy - lam_s * sum_y)
logw = loglik - loglik.max()                     # for numerical stability
w_g = np.exp(logw)
w_g_norm = w_g / w_g.sum()

post_mean_nu = np.sum(nu_s * w_g_norm)
post_mean_lam = np.sum(lam_s * w_g_norm)
ess_g = 1.0 / np.sum(w_g_norm ** 2)
print(f"simulated discharge: n={n_obs}, mean={y_disch.mean():.3f} "
      f"(true nu/lambda = {nu_true/lam_true:.3f})")
print(f"posterior mean: nu = {post_mean_nu:.3f} (true {nu_true}), "
      f"lambda = {post_mean_lam:.3f} (true {lam_true})")
print(f"effective sample size: {ess_g:.0f} out of {S_g}")
```

The simulated series has a mean close to the model's implied $\nu/\lambda = 1.5$, and
both posterior means land close to the parameters that generated the data, recovering
the truth the same way the beta-binomial and truncated-normal examples did earlier, this
time for a genuinely two-dimensional, non-conjugate model. The effective sample size is
far below $S_g$, because the prior is much more diffuse than the likelihood and so is a
poor match to it as a proposal; this is the price of the shortcut, paid here in wasted
draws rather than in a wrong answer, and it is exactly the kind of situation the next
lectures address with proposals that adapt to the posterior instead of ignoring it.

The posterior predictive probability that a *future* discharge exceeds some threshold is
now one line of simulation once we have weighted parameter draws: for each
$(\nu^{(s)}, \lambda^{(s)})$ draw one predictive value $Y^{(s)} \sim
\text{Gamma}(\nu^{(s)}, 1/\lambda^{(s)})$ and average the indicator that it exceeds the
threshold, using the same self-normalised weights as before. This is the discrete Monte
Carlo version of $\Pr(Y_{n+1} > c \mid y) = \int \Pr(Y_{n+1}>c \mid \nu,\lambda)\,
p(\nu,\lambda\mid y)\, d\nu\, d\lambda$.

```{python}
y_pred = rng.gamma(shape=nu_s, scale=1 / lam_s)          # one draw per (nu, lambda)
threshold = 3.0                                          # twice the model's mean discharge

pred_prob = np.sum((y_pred > threshold) * w_g_norm)
print(f"P(future discharge > {threshold} | data)  ~=  {pred_prob:.4f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(y_disch, bins=25, density=True, alpha=0.5, label="observed discharge")
ax.hist(y_pred, bins=200, weights=w_g_norm, range=(0, 8), density=True,
        histtype="step", lw=2, label="posterior predictive")
ax.axvline(threshold, color="black", ls=":", label=f"threshold = {threshold}")
ax.set_xlabel("discharge"); ax.set_ylabel("density"); ax.set_xlim(0, 8)
ax.legend(); ax.set_title("Posterior predictive distribution of future discharge")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The predictive histogram is visibly wider than the observed data's own spread, because
it carries parameter uncertainty on top of the sampling variability the gamma model
already implies, exactly the effect Lecture 1's beta-binomial predictive illustrated in
the coin example. The printed probability of exceeding the threshold is the number a
hydrologist or a risk manager would actually want, and it required no closed form
anywhere in the calculation, only the weighted Monte Carlo average of an indicator.

## Vanilla Monte Carlo for option pricing under parameter uncertainty

The paired exercise for this week is to price a financial option by simulation while
letting the model's volatility parameter carry its own posterior uncertainty, which is
the plain Monte Carlo idea from the start of the lecture applied to a genuinely
practical problem: averaging a function of simulated paths, where now one of the
"random draws" is a parameter rather than data. Under the standard geometric Brownian
motion model, a stock with current price $S_0$, risk-free rate $r$ and volatility
$\sigma$ has a terminal price after time $T$ given by
$S_T = S_0 \exp\!\big((r - \sigma^2/2)T + \sigma\sqrt{T}\,Z\big)$ for $Z \sim
\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, and the fair price of a European call with strike $K$ is the
discounted expected payoff, $e^{-rT}\mathbb{E}[\max(S_T - K, 0)]$, which is itself an
integral over $Z$ that Monte Carlo estimates by simulating many paths and averaging the
payoff. The textbook version of this calculation treats $\sigma$ as known. In practice
it is estimated from historical returns and therefore uncertain, and that uncertainty
should propagate into the option price rather than being discarded by plugging in a
point estimate.

We generate a short history of daily log-returns from a "true" volatility, then use the
normal-model conjugate result for the variance (the same normal-inverse-gamma family
referenced in Lecture 2) to get a posterior distribution over $\sigma^2$ instead of a
single number: with a $\text{Gamma}(a_0, b_0)$ prior on the precision $1/\sigma^2$ and
$m$ observed returns with sum of squares $\text{SS}$, the posterior is $1/\sigma^2 \mid
\text{data} \sim \text{Gamma}(a_0 + m/2,\, b_0 + \text{SS}/2)$, mirroring exactly the
Poisson-gamma update of Lecture 1. With that posterior in hand we price a one-year
at-the-money European call two ways: the naive plug-in approach that fixes $\sigma$ at
its posterior mean before simulating, and the full Bayesian approach that draws a fresh
$\sigma$ from its posterior for every simulated path, so parameter uncertainty and
sampling uncertainty are mixed together exactly as the predictive distribution mixed
them in the discharge example.

```{python}
sigma_true_daily = 0.02
returns = rng.normal(0, sigma_true_daily, size=250)          # one year of daily returns
a0, b0 = 2.0, 0.0005
m, SS = returns.size, (returns ** 2).sum()
post_precision = stats.gamma(a0 + m / 2, scale=1 / (b0 + SS / 2))

S_opt = 50_000
sigma_daily_draws = 1 / np.sqrt(post_precision.rvs(size=S_opt, random_state=rng))
sigma_annual_draws = sigma_daily_draws * np.sqrt(252)

S0, K, r, T = 100.0, 100.0, 0.02, 1.0
Z = rng.standard_normal(S_opt)
sigma_bar = sigma_annual_draws.mean()
ST_plugin = S0 * np.exp((r - sigma_bar**2/2)*T + sigma_bar*np.sqrt(T)*Z)
price_plugin = np.exp(-r*T) * np.maximum(ST_plugin - K, 0).mean()
ST_full = S0 * np.exp((r - sigma_annual_draws**2/2)*T
                       + sigma_annual_draws*np.sqrt(T)*Z)
price_full = np.exp(-r*T) * np.maximum(ST_full - K, 0).mean()

print(f"posterior mean annualised volatility: {sigma_bar:.4f} "
      f"(true {sigma_true_daily*np.sqrt(252):.4f})")
print(f"plug-in price (fixed sigma = posterior mean): {price_plugin:.4f}")
print(f"full Bayesian price (sigma drawn per path):    {price_full:.4f}")
print(f"price increase from pricing in parameter uncertainty: "
      f"{100*(price_full/price_plugin - 1):.2f}%")
```

The full Bayesian price comes out slightly above the plug-in price, and the direction
is not an accident: the option payoff is a convex function of volatility, so by
Jensen's inequality $\mathbb{E}_\sigma[\text{price}(\sigma)] \geq
\text{price}(\mathbb{E}[\sigma])$ whenever price is convex in $\sigma$, and averaging
over the posterior of $\sigma$ rather than plugging in its mean can only push the price
up, never down. The gap is small here because a full year of daily returns pins
$\sigma$ down fairly precisely, so its posterior is tight and the plug-in price is
already close to the full average; with less data, or a more diffuse prior, the same
convexity acts on a wider spread of $\sigma$ and the gap widens, which is exactly what
Exercise 5 asks you to check. The general point survives the small size of the number
here: ignoring parameter uncertainty does not just add noise around the right answer,
it produces an estimate that is systematically too low, which is why risk desks that
treat volatility as known tend to under-price optionality. Both simulations are
otherwise identical vanilla Monte Carlo, exactly the machinery of the lecture's first
section, applied to a payoff function instead of a posterior summary.

## Takeaways

Posterior summaries are integrals, and outside conjugate models those integrals are
intractable, with quadrature failing exponentially fast as the number of parameters
grows. Monte Carlo integration replaces the integral with a sample average that is
unbiased by linearity of expectation and consistent by the law of large numbers, with an
error that shrinks like $1/\sqrt{S}$ regardless of dimension. When we cannot sample the
target directly, importance sampling reweights draws from a proposal by the ratio of
target to proposal density, exactly and without approximation, and its self-normalised
version trades a vanishing finite-sample bias for working with an unnormalised target;
its reliability depends entirely on the proposal having heavier tails than the target,
which the effective sample size lets us monitor. Rejection sampling instead accepts or
discards proposal draws geometrically to return exact draws from the target, at a cost
that grows quickly with dimension, and sampling-importance-resampling converts a
weighted sample into an approximately unweighted one as a bridge to the adaptive
samplers ahead. The gamma and option-pricing examples showed the same machinery solving
two applied problems: predicting a positive-valued series and pricing an option while
carrying parameter uncertainty all the way through to the final number, rather than
discarding it at a plug-in estimate.
